title: Turn, Turn, Turn
theme: The roots vert and vers: turning
objectives: I can use the roots vert and vers (turn) to work out the meaning of ten words.
I can explain how prefixes such as con-, di-, a-, re-, in-, ad-, contro-, and intro- steer the turn.
I can tell apart close pairs such as avert and divert, or revert and reverse, by using context.
I can write about a disagreement or a change using words built on vert and vers.
rationale: Vert and vers (turn) show how one physical picture grows into abstract meanings: turning into something new (convert), turning aside (divert), turning away to stop something (avert), turning back (revert, reverse), turning upside down (invert), turning against (adverse, controversy), turning inward (introvert), and turning easily (versatile). The unit sits after the c-e-d roots so that students already expect a root plus a prefix and can predict the meaning before checking context. Avert and adverse are flagged as confusable because they sound alike and look like avoid and averse. Oppress, reform, and escalate return from the civics and conflict units so students can describe how a disagreement grows or changes.

words.def: To change something into a different form or use.

senses.def: A person who has changed from one belief or practice to another.
senses.example: As a new convert to vegetarian cooking, Lia tried a different bean recipe every night.

words.ex: The town decided to convert the old train station into a farmers' market.
words.ex2: A solar panel converts sunlight into electricity.
words.nonExample: Leaving a building exactly as it is does not convert it into anything.

apps.academic: In math class, you convert fractions to decimals and miles to kilometers.
apps.spoken: Can you convert this recipe from cups to grams?
apps.writing: Use convert when something changes into a new form or use.

cloze.s: The charity plans to ___ the empty warehouse into a shelter for families.

cloze2.s: A calculator can ___ miles into kilometers in a second.

misuse.s: To convert the garage into a gym, she left it exactly as it was, with the same shelves and boxes.
misuse.why: To convert is to change something into a new form or use; leaving it unchanged does not do that.

visual.alt: A circular arrow beside a factory building.

words.def: To turn something away from its course or purpose toward another.
words.ex: Workers dug a channel to divert the river around the village.
words.ex2: The magician used a loud clap to divert everyone's attention from his other hand.
words.nonExample: Water that keeps flowing down its original path has not been diverted.

apps.academic: Engineers divert floodwater to protect towns near rivers.
apps.spoken: We had to divert from the main road because of construction.
apps.writing: Use divert for moving a path, money, or attention to another place.

cloze.s: The police had to ___ traffic onto side streets while crews repaired the broken bridge.

cloze2.s: Engineers built a canal to ___ floodwater away from the houses at the edge of town.

misuse.s: The crew diverted the traffic by letting every car continue along its original route.
misuse.why: To divert is to turn something away from its route; letting cars keep their route is not diverting.

visual.alt: A construction barrier with an arrow showing a new route.

words.def: To prevent something bad from happening.

senses.def: To turn your eyes or your thoughts away.
senses.example: She averted her eyes when the scene on the screen became too scary.

words.ex: A quick-thinking driver averted a crash by braking just in time.
words.ex2: Last-minute talks averted a strike that would have closed every school in the city.
words.nonExample: A firefighter who arrives after a building has burned has not averted a disaster.

apps.academic: Careful planning can avert a shortage of supplies during a crisis.
apps.spoken: Thank goodness we averted a disaster with that phone call.
apps.writing: Use avert for stopping a bad outcome; do not use it for stopping a good one.

cloze.s: Quick action by the lifeguard ___ a tragedy when he pulled the swimmer out of the current.

cloze2.s: The two leaders met late into the night to ___ a war that seemed certain.

misuse.s: The lifeguard averted the accident by watching it happen and doing nothing.
misuse.why: To avert is to prevent something bad; doing nothing does not prevent it.

visual.alt: A stop sign in front of a car that has halted.

words.def: To go back to an earlier state, habit, or condition.
words.ex: After the vacation, the students reverted to their usual morning routine.
words.ex2: If you stop watering it, the green lawn will revert to dry brown dirt.
words.nonExample: A plant that keeps growing taller is moving forward, not reverting.
words.rel: turning back to how it was

apps.academic: A stream may revert to its old path after a flood ends.
apps.spoken: I tried to stop biting my nails, but I reverted to the habit during exams.
apps.writing: Use revert for a return to a former condition, especially a worse one.

cloze.s: When the heat wave ended, the temperature began to ___ to its normal range for spring.

cloze2.s: He worked hard to stop biting his nails, but under stress he would ___ to the old habit.

misuse.s: The garden reverted to a wild field because it was weeded and replanted every week.
misuse.why: To revert is to go back to an earlier state; careful weeding and planting keeps a garden tended, not wild.

visual.alt: A curved arrow pointing back toward a patch of weeds.

words.frame: After ___, we tended to revert to ___.

words.def: To turn something upside down or reverse its usual order.
words.ex: To empty the last drops, he inverted the bottle over the sink.
words.ex2: Mathematicians invert a fraction by switching the numerator and the denominator.
words.nonExample: A glass sitting upright on a shelf has not been inverted.

apps.academic: To divide by a fraction, you invert it and then multiply.
apps.spoken: Invert the bowl onto a plate and the pudding will slide out.
apps.writing: Use invert for flipping an object or the usual order of something.

cloze.s: To shape the sandcastle, she filled the bucket with wet sand and then ___ it onto the beach.

cloze2.s: Poets sometimes ___ the normal order of words in a line to create a surprising rhythm.

misuse.s: She inverted the picture by hanging it exactly as it was, with the sky at the top.
misuse.why: To invert is to turn something upside down; leaving the sky at the top is not inverting.

visual.alt: An upside-down face next to a glass of milk.

words.def: To turn something the other way round, or to change it to the opposite.

senses.def: The opposite of what was just said or done.
senses.example: The result was the reverse of what the team had expected.

words.ex: Reverse the order of the steps, and the recipe no longer works.
words.ex2: The judge reversed the earlier decision after seeing new evidence.
words.nonExample: Repeating the same decision a second time does not reverse it.

morph.note: The root vers is written with a final e in this word (vers -> verse).

apps.academic: A court of appeals can reverse the decision of a lower court.
apps.spoken: Can you reverse the car out of the driveway so I can load the trunk?
apps.writing: Use reverse for turning around or changing to the opposite, not for small edits.

cloze.s: The coach decided to ___ the batting order, putting the last hitter first and the first hitter last.

cloze2.s: A higher court may ___ a verdict if the first trial was found to be unfair.

misuse.s: She reversed her opinion by repeating exactly what she had said before.
misuse.why: To reverse an opinion is to change to the opposite; repeating the same words does not.

visual.alt: A looping arrow beside a car.

words.def: A public argument about something that many people disagree on.
words.ex: A controversy erupted when the council proposed closing the neighborhood pool.
words.ex2: The film caused controversy because some viewers thought it showed history unfairly.
words.nonExample: A question that everyone answers the same way is not a controversy.

apps.academic: Historians describe the controversy over how the law should be applied.
apps.spoken: That topic always causes a controversy at my family's dinner table.
apps.writing: Use controversy for a public disagreement, not for a private quarrel.

cloze.s: The new dress code started a ___ that divided parents, teachers, and students.

cloze2.s: Because the issue was a ___, newspaper editors printed opinions from both sides.

misuse.s: There was no controversy at all, because every person in the room strongly disagreed with every other.
misuse.why: A controversy is a public argument; everyone disagreeing is exactly that, not the absence of one.

visual.alt: A speaking face beside a balance scale.

words.frame: The controversy over ___ divided people because ___.

words.def: Harmful or unfavorable; working against what you want to happen.
words.ex: Adverse weather forced the crew to postpone the rescue until morning.
words.ex2: Doctors watch for adverse reactions when a patient starts a new medicine.
words.nonExample: Sunny, calm weather is not adverse for a picnic.

morph.note: The root vers is written with a final e in this word (vers -> verse).

apps.academic: Scientists record any adverse effects that appear during an experiment.
apps.spoken: The adverse conditions made the hike much harder than planned.
apps.writing: Use adverse for conditions or effects; use averse for a person who dislikes something.

cloze.s: The soccer match was canceled because of ___ conditions: heavy rain and a strong wind.

cloze2.s: Smoke from the fire had an ___ effect on people with asthma.

misuse.s: The adverse weather was perfect for the parade, with sunshine and a gentle breeze.
misuse.why: Adverse means harmful or unfavorable; sunshine and a gentle breeze are favorable.

visual.alt: A storm cloud beside a warning sign.

words.frame: Adverse conditions such as ___ can make ___.

words.def: Able to do many different things or be used in many ways.
words.ex: A versatile player can take any position on the soccer field.
words.ex2: A plain white shirt is versatile because it goes with almost any outfit.
words.nonExample: A tool that can only do one narrow job is not versatile.

morph.note: The e of -ate is dropped before -ile.

words.rel: able to turn to many uses

apps.academic: A versatile writer can adjust style for a news story, a poem, or a lab report.
apps.spoken: That jacket is so versatile; I wear it everywhere.
apps.writing: Use versatile for a person or a thing that adapts well to many situations.

cloze.s: The ___ actor played a villain, a comedian, and a hero in the same season.

cloze2.s: A sturdy backpack is ___, since it works for school, for hikes, and for short trips.

misuse.s: The versatile knife could do only one job and nothing else.
misuse.why: Versatile means able to do many things; a knife that does one job is the opposite.

visual.alt: A toolbox beside two theater masks.

words.def: A person who prefers quiet time alone or with a few close friends.
words.ex: Although she is an introvert, Maya loves long talks with her two best friends.
words.ex2: As an introvert, Theo recharges by reading alone after a busy school day.
words.nonExample: Someone who feels energized by large parties is not an introvert.

apps.academic: Psychologists describe introverts as people who feel recharged by quiet time.
apps.spoken: I'm an introvert, so I need some quiet time after a big party.
apps.writing: Use introvert for a person's style; it does not mean the person is shy or unfriendly.

cloze.s: As an ___, Elena felt tired after the crowded party and wanted a quiet evening with a book.

cloze2.s: The ___ on the team preferred to send her ideas in writing rather than speak in the large meeting.

misuse.s: An introvert is a person who gets the most energy from loud crowds and never wants to be alone.
misuse.why: An introvert prefers quiet time alone or with a few friends; loving crowds describes the opposite.

visual.alt: An open book on a quiet sofa.

words.frame: An introvert might choose to ___ instead of ___.

passage.title: The Gym Debate
paras: When the school board announced plans to convert the old gym into a library, the whole town of Millbrook split into two camps. Some neighbors cheered. Others remembered fifty years of basketball games and Friday dances. By Monday the controversy had reached the school newspaper, and its editor, Dara, knew her team had to cover it fairly.

Her best writer was Sam, a quiet introvert who preferred listening to talking. Dara worried that interviews would be hard for him, but Sam surprised her. He was versatile: he could write a news story, draw a map of the proposed library, and photograph the crowd. "Interviewing is just listening with a notebook," he told her.

At the board meeting, the mood turned tense. One parent complained that the gym could never again be used for sports. Another said the project would divert money from the bus budget. A third warned that a rushed vote might have adverse effects on students who relied on after-school programs. The board president tried to avert an angry shouting match by reminding everyone that each speaker would get two minutes.

Sam recorded every point, and he noticed something unexpected. When people really listened, some began to reverse their positions. The parent worried about sports agreed that a library could hold evening homework clubs. Later, though, when one speaker called the plan wasteful, several people seemed ready to revert to their first arguments, as if the meeting had spun back to its starting point.

For Friday's paper, Dara chose to invert the usual layout. Instead of opening with the board's statement, the front page began with three questions from readers, and the answers appeared beneath. Teachers stopped her in the hallway to say they liked it. The debate was not over, but students on both sides said they finally understood what the other side feared.

qs.q: In paragraph 3, the phrase "divert money from the bus budget" means to
choices: add more money to the bus budget
send the money to a different use
count the money again
give the money back to families
qs.why: To divert is to turn something from its course; the parent is saying the money would go to the library instead of the buses.

qs.q: Why does Dara call Sam "versatile" in the story, even though he is quiet?
choices: He can do several different jobs well for the newspaper.
He refuses to speak at the board meeting.
He wants to be the editor himself.
He changes his opinion about the library.
qs.why: The passage says he can write, draw a map, and take photographs, which shows he can do many different things.

qs.q: In paragraph 4, what does "revert to their first arguments" suggest?
choices: People moved on to completely new arguments.
People went back to the arguments they had made before.
People refused to say anything more.
People agreed with the library plan.
qs.why: The text says the meeting seemed to spin back to its starting point, which matches going back to earlier arguments.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that the board president tried to prevent trouble?
choices: She called the plan wasteful.
She asked that each speaker get only two minutes.
She printed the paper on Friday.
She moved the meeting to the old gym.
qs.why: Limiting speakers to two minutes was her attempt to avert an angry shouting match.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses a central idea of the passage?
choices: Newspapers should not cover local debates.
Listening to different sides can help people understand a controversy even when they still disagree.
Libraries are more important than gyms.
A rushed vote always gives the best result.
qs.why: Sam notices that listening changes some minds, and students on both sides say they understand the other side after the paper runs both views.

argue.frame: I believe that schools should ___ because ___. An introvert would ___, and a versatile space could ___.

constructed.prompt: A flood is coming toward a town. Explain what workers could do with a river and what the goal would be, using divert and avert.
look: shows that divert moves the water's path
shows that avert prevents the damage
constructed.model: Workers could divert the river into a wide channel so the water avoids the streets. That would avert a flood and keep homes dry.

shows that reverse means change to the opposite

teacher.overview: Students use the roots vert and vers (turn) and eight prefixes to unlock ten words, read a short narrative about a community debate, and practice choosing between close pairs. The big idea is that a root gives a picture and a prefix gives a direction, so students can predict meanings before they check context.

notes.va.convert.v: Two senses: the verb (change into) and the noun convert (a person who changed beliefs). Use math conversions as the concrete picture. The prefix con- is glossed here as together or completely; students do not need more than that.
notes.va.divert.v: Pair with avert: divert changes a path, avert prevents a bad result. Use a map with a closed road and an arrow. Students often choose divert when avert fits the sentence better.
notes.va.avert.v: Confusable with avoid and with adverse. Avert prevents something bad; avoid keeps away from it. The second sense (avert your eyes) is taught as a sense but practice stays on prevent. Do not claim a history beyond the root.
notes.va.revert.v: Re- (back) plus vert (turn). Students often say revert when they mean reverse. Use a before-and-after drawing of a lawn that returns to dirt.
notes.va.invert.v: Picture a glass turned upside down. In math, invert a fraction to divide by it. In writing, poets sometimes invert word order. Check that students can describe the direction of the turn.
notes.va.reverse.v: Multiple meaning: reverse as a verb (turn around, change to the opposite) and the noun the reverse. Stress is on the second syllable for the verb. Spell reverse with the e and note that the root vers adds an e here.
notes.va.controversy.n: Contro- (against) plus vers (turn) plus -y. Use a real neutral local issue such as school start times. Ask students to say what two sides disagree about before using the word.
notes.va.adverse.adj: Confusable with averse (a person who dislikes something). Show that adverse describes conditions or effects: adverse weather, adverse reaction. Model a quick check: is it about a person or a thing?
notes.va.versatile.adj: Students may not see vers here. Explain that the root appears inside a longer ending; do not teach more history than needed. Ask students to name versatile objects in the classroom.
notes.va.introvert.n: Intro- (inward) plus vert (turn). Avoid labeling a student as introverted or extroverted; use fictional examples. Stress that introvert describes how a person recharges, not a lack of friends or skills.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'I see vert in revert and invert. Vert means turn. Re- means back, so revert means turn back to an earlier state. In- can mean in or toward, and invert means to turn something upside down. The sentence says a lawn reverts to dry dirt, so revert fits: it goes back to how it was before.'
discuss: Which word from the unit describes you on a busy day, and why?
How can a prefix turn the same root toward, away, or back?
misconceptions: Revert and reverse are the same word.
An introvert is shy or has no friends.
Divert and avert both mean stop something bad.
extend: Find vert or vers words in a science or social studies chapter and sort them by prefix.
Write a short scene in which a character must avert a disaster and a friend must divert attention at a key moment.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Return to avert/divert and revert/reverse as contrast pairs after two days and again at one week. Revisit oppress, reform, and escalate by asking students to describe how a disagreement could escalate or be reformed in a short paragraph.

frames: To divert is to ___, but to avert is to ___.
I think ___ is a controversy because people disagree about ___.
wida.oral: Partner A acts out or describes one vert or vers word without saying it (for example, flipping a cup over); Partner B names the word and the prefix that gives its direction.

needsReview: Spanish glosses (desviar, evitar, revertir, invertir for both invert and reverse, versátil, introvertido) not reviewed by a native speaker; invertir covers reverse only loosely, and revertir is less common in everyday Spanish.

Prefix meanings are simplified teaching glosses: con- (together; completely), in- (in; toward), ad- (toward), a- (away); no origin claims are made. Versatile is segmented as vers + -ate + -ile for teaching; confirm the segmentation against a dictionary.
Sense boundaries: convert, avert, and reverse each carry a second sense; practice stays on the first sense.
